title: SEC weighs one-year sit-out rule for intra-conference transfers
dek: The SEC is weighing a proposal to require athletes who transfer to another school within the conference to sit out one season, a move aimed at controlling player movement after the spring transfer portal window was eliminated. The policy would face likely legal challenges and could push top talent to leave the conference entirely.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: SEC presidents are considering a new policy requiring intra-conference transfers to sit out one season, leaning on an old NCAA rule structure.
bottom_line: The outcome hinges on whether SEC presidents vote to adopt the rule and, if they do, whether courts allow it to stand. A successful court challenge would force the SEC to abandon the policy; acceptance by the judiciary would test whether the deterrent actually keeps talent in the conference or simply accelerates departures to other leagues.
body: The SEC is considering a new policy that would require athletes transferring to another conference school to sit out one season, according to CBS Sports. SEC presidents plan to meet to weigh the proposal as the conference moves to control internal player movement in the transfer era.

The sit-out mandate would apply only to transfers within the SEC. According to CBS Sports, the policy borrows from an old NCAA rule structure that required all undergraduate transfers to sit out a season unless they received a waiver.

The timing of the proposal reflects changes to the transfer landscape. The spring transfer portal window has been eliminated, per CBS Sports. In previous years, when two portal windows existed, players could not transfer within their own conference during the spring cycle. The new policy would extend that deterrent year-round by adding a mandatory sit-out period.

The rule would aim to reduce what CBS Sports describes as conference teams poaching players from one another. However, the strategy carries a built-in risk: top transfer candidates in the SEC may be more inclined to leave the conference altogether in favor of premier programs in other leagues rather than accept a season of ineligibility, according to CBS Sports reporting.

The SEC's move toward self-governance comes as the Protect College Sports Act, which recently passed the Senate, still faces hurdles in the House, per CBS Sports. Any new transfer policy adopted in modern college athletics would almost certainly be tested in court, according to CBS Sports, adding legal uncertainty to the proposal if adopted.
